The Black pomfret Parastromateus niger is a commercially important carangid fish distributed throughout the Indo-West Pacific region, where it supports substantial fisheries. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies have provided a comprehensive picture of its life history traits, revealing a maximum recorded fork length of 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters] for the largest individuals captured. The species exhibits relatively rapid early growth, with yolk-sac larvae transitioning to exogenous feeding shortly after hatching. Under controlled rearing conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], the period from fertilisation to hatching is completed in approximately 3.2 days [ab = approximately 3.2 days], a developmental duration consistent with that of other tropical carangids of comparable egg size. This brief embryonic phase is followed by a lecithotrophic larval stage during which the alevin relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of active prey capture.

Newly hatched prolarvae of Parastromateus niger are initially minute, with an estimated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a value reflecting the modest egg diameter of roughly one millimeter. This low initial mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum among carangid larvae. Throughout the planktonic larval phase, rapid somatic growth and morphological transformation occur, culminating in larval metamorphosis and the transition to a benthic juvenile stage. The individuals gradually accumulate body mass, and studies based on length-weight regressions indicate that adult fish can attain a substantial ultimate wet weight of 6740 grams [Wwi = 6740 grams]. This represents a dramatic increase over the birth mass, highlighting the species' significant growth potential under favorable oceanic conditions.

This threshold marks the attainment of puberty in both sexes, after which individuals are physiologically capable of participating in spawning aggregations. The species is iteroparous and exhibits a defined spawning season. Females produce approximately 18,975 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 18,975 eggs per spawning event] and can release up to eight batches of eggs annually [F_R_i = up to eight batches of eggs annually], collectively constituting an extraordinary capacity for population replenishment when compared to other carangids of similar body size.

Lifespan estimates for Parastromateus niger have been derived from otolith increment analyses and mark-recapture studies conducted across its geographical range. The maximum documented longevity for wild individuals reared at the average ambient temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] is approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days], equivalent to a decade of life. This lifespan is moderate for a carangid of its ultimate size, reflecting a life history strategy that balances relatively rapid maturation with sustained reproductive output over several years. The species experiences natural mortality primarily from predation by larger pelagic fishes during the larval and juvenile stages, with senescence and age-related physiological deterioration contributing to death in the oldest members of the population.
